newsitem.title: USA: NASD to end mandatory arbitration for bias cases.
newsitem.headline: NASD to end mandatory arbitration for bias cases.

text.p: The National Association of Securities Dealers has decided to end a Wall Street policy that prevents employees of securities firms from taking their discrimination and harassment claims to court.
Under its latest proposals approved Thursday, the association would stop requiring that workers in securities firms agree to arbitrate all job discrimination claims.
"For cases that allege a violation of a person's civil rights, employees will have the choice to have their claim heard in court," Frank Zarb, NASD chairman, said.
Individual firms, however, would still be able to force their employees to arbitrate claims as a condition of employment, opponents of the arbitration-only requirement say.

"It certainly is a start, but there are an awful lot of employers imposing these agreements just as a condition of employment," said Cynthia Misicka, a top attorney at the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which blasted the industry practice. "It's an issue very near and dear to our hearts," she said.
Under current rules for NASD, the securities industry's self regulator, individuals working for securities firms are required to arbitrate all claims.
Securities industry leaders say the arbitration process works well and should not be changed.

But opponents of the arbitration-only requirement say the practice prevents women, minorities and older workers on Wall Street from enjoying the same protections U.S. law gives to every other U.S. worker.
Patricia Ireland, president of the National Organisation for Women, appauded the NASD's latest move but agreed that more work in the securities industry is needed.
"It's a very satisfying benchmark, it's not the end of the campaign. Now we have the opportunity to work on convincing one or more of the big firms to open the door further," she said.
Ireland's organisation will address corporate boards of directors and others about changing the practice, she said.

Discrimination or sexual harassment claims made up less than 2 percent of the cases filed last year with the NASD. But the issue has attracted widespread attention in recent months, following high profile cases involving Smith Barney and Merrill Lynch & Co.

"The NASD's mandatory arbitration policy added insult to injury for women who were sexually harassed or otherwise discriminated at work," said Helen Norton, director of equal opportunity programmes at the Women's Legal Defence Fund.
The new NASD rules would be effective a year after the SEC approves them, the association said.

In addition to ending the arbitration-only requirement, the NASD said it will continue improving its arbitration system by making sure the panels hearing cases are more diverse and better trained to handle discrimination claims.

The Securities Industry Association in a statement said it still supports the use of mandatory arbitration. "We are disappointed in the NASD's decision today because we feel the facts show the current system workes well," the group's general counsel, Stuart Kaswell, said in a statement.
"While we have no immediate plans for change, we intend to study the details of the NASD's proposals," a Merrill Lynch spokeswoman said.
